# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Walks the owner through what waits on him, one decision at a time, and records each answer where it belongs. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Build the queue. The command lists each decision once: requirements waiting for approval, proposed designs, results at stage 11, Open Questions rows the owner decides, and memory proposals. Its "Agent to-do" lines are not decisions. A delivery offer belongs to `work-delegate`: open it after his other decisions.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. He gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision; when two could match, ask which, naming both. A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" with no question asked is not an answer (`references/approvals.md`, section 1).
3. Otherwise start with the count and one short line for every waiting decision, memory proposals included ("3 decisions wait on you: the WI-004 design, the WI-006 result, and a memory proposal about deploy days."). Then take them one at a time, the one blocking the most work first: what is decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. One decision per message, in the reply text.
4. An approval: read the item, then run that gate's checklist in `references/approvals.md` (requirements: section 2; design: section 3; result: section 4).
   `toolkit work show <id>`
5. An Open Questions answer: save his words first, rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and Answered, then set `waiting_on` back (`references/recording-owner-answers.md`, sections 4 and 5).
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect '<what the answer changes>'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
6. A memory proposal: show its one line and your recommendation. Yes: approve it. No: reject it, and never propose the same fact again (`references/proposals.md`).
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory reject <key>`
7. A decision for the whole project: add the row inside the `publish-docs` save workspace, in the order in `references/decisions-log.md`.
   `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>`
8. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
9. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. Update the current focus when an answer changed an item's next step (`references/current-focus.md`). After each recorded answer, list the decisions again and name what still waits on him, memory proposals included, by name ("One decision still waits: the memory proposal about Ghost slugs."). A decision an earlier reply said you would take next is taken next. Empty queue: say so and offer `work-on` for unblocked items. End with the next decision's question or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work decisions`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue. A bare question is not enough.
- Ask in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- The approve command marks the Open Questions rows that asked for it Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered". Never edit those rows again by hand.
- `waiting_on`: `agent` when the agent continues, `none` when nothing waits, `owner` while another of his questions on that item is still open. The approve command sets `none` by itself.
- A memory proposal is not a fact until he approves it. Do not rely on it.
- An approval never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- After a result approval, the item continues with `work-finish`. Open it when he wants it shipped now.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Build the queue from the labels in `references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`, and remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer.

## Example decision message

```markdown
WI-015 needs your choice of design.

- Option A: use the built-in report page. Ready in about a day; the layout is fixed.
- Option B: a custom page. About a week; any layout you want.

I recommend A, because every requirement is met without custom code.
After A: I plan the build. After B: I plan a longer build and ask you about the layout.

Do you approve Option A?
```

# Work requirements

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Interviews the owner and writes what the result must do, never how to build it; every answer lands in the work item. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does; none exists, create it with his words as the Starting request. Requirements already approved and no change asked: open the skill the item's "Continue with" names and stop.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Starting request' --text '<his exact words>'`
2. Move it to refinement once requirements are being written. Before the first question, read the item and what the project already knows (`references/interview.md`, section 2).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
3. Restate the goal in one sentence ("So the goal is X?"). Write the Agreed goal after a yes, and always before asking for approval.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Agreed goal' --text '<goal>'`
4. Ask one question at a time, most basic first, each with a recommended answer and a short reason (`references/interview.md`, sections 3 and 4).
5. Save each answer before the next question: `R-xx` blocks and the Acceptance list in the format in `references/requirement-format.md`; anything unanswered as an Open Questions row, with the item waiting on the owner while one of his is open.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Active requirements' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
6. A change to an approved requirement: edit the `R-xx`, keep the old wording in its Decision record, set it back to Refining, move the item to refinement, and say what the change affects when the item is past stage 03 (`references/interview.md`, section 7). The earlier approval stays on the record, and the stage command says so: it covered the requirements as they were, so ask him to approve the changed ones (step 8) before anything is built on them.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
7. Spec check, before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the spec": brief the `requirements-analyst` and handle its findings (`references/spec-check.md`).
8. Ask for approval and record his yes with the requirements checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 2. Then a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless he agreed to skip the design.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
9. Lead with "Not saved" on a failed write. Validate, update the current focus when the next step changed (`references/current-focus.md`), and hand back to `work-on` unless the owner stops. End with the one question or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Ask in the reply text, never through a question tool. "Grill me" or "ask me questions" means one question at a time, never a batch.
- Build ideas never go into requirements: they go under Notes > Solution options and considerations.
- The CLI refuses the approval while the Agreed goal still holds the template text.
- Local and Notion trackers: never write the Requirements "Overall status" line; the approve command sets it. GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so there the agent writes it after his yes.
- A change to an approved `R-xx` sends the item back to refinement and needs approval again.
- The spec check changes nothing without the owner's yes.
- "Give me options first" is not a requirements approval: go to `solution-design` with the open choices kept visible.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Edit the issue's Requirements section as `references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md` says.

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst` (`references/agent-requirements-analyst.md`): the spec check in step 7. The brief is in `references/spec-check.md`.
- `researcher` (`references/agent-researcher.md`): one per fact the owner cannot answer (a platform limit, what the existing build does).
- Brief them as `references/helpers.md` says.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. # Recording the owner's answers

Where each thing the owner says is saved, how to ask him a question, how to
end a reply, and what to say when a save fails.

## Contents

1. Voice
2. Where each answer goes
3. Save it before the next question
4. History notes
5. Waiting on the owner
6. Asking the owner
7. Ending every reply
8. Reporting a failed save
9. Owner edits win
10. Stages in plain words
11. Handing over to another skill

## 1. Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Helper agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file carries its
own writing rules.

## 2. Where each answer goes

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Active requirements` (the `R-xx` block) and `Acceptance` | The new meaning, and Status Refining until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer |
| Answer or decision about this item | The question's row, the section it changes, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| Context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to |
| A lasting fact, preference, or lesson | Project memory, through `memory-save` | One record |

A choice about how agents deliver a goal (the delivery offer) is recorded
only by `work-delegate`.

## 3. Save it before the next question

- Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
  unanswered question is also information: save it as an Open Questions row.
- Open decisions never delay saving answers that are already settled.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.
- Check the item and memory before asking the owner something. Never ask
  again what the record already answers.
- When two sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Never pick the
  convenient answer.

## 4. History notes

Add one note when:

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who; do not claim you checked
  it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

```text
toolkit work history <id> --note '<what happened>' --effect '<what it changes>'
```

- Without `--effect`, the row names the skill that continues the item. A note
  that quotes the owner right after an approval or a `waiting_on` change
  needs its own `--effect`: the default is worked out from the item before the
  change and can name the wrong next step.
- Record the owner's meaning briefly. Add no reason, scope, or certainty he
  did not give.
- A note that quotes him starts with `Owner said:`, followed by his words in
  double quotes inside the single-quoted text. A quote is his exact words:
  never reword it to avoid an apostrophe ("she'll" stays "she'll", never
  "she will").
- Keep apostrophes out of your own words in the note where you can. In a
  quote, and wherever one is needed, write it as `'\''` in Claude Code and as
  ’ (U+2019) in Codex (`toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs, or small
  edits.

Examples:

```text
toolkit work history WI-012 --note 'Owner said: "yes, approved"' --effect 'Requirements approved; solution-design continues.'
toolkit work history WI-012 --note 'Build found the export API has a 10,000-row limit.' --effect 'P2 added for paged exports.'
```

## 5. Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask him for an approval, or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
  `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
- `toolkit work approve` sets `waiting_on` from `owner` to `none`, because he
  just answered. Then set it to `agent` when the agent continues.
  `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- After he answers his last open question on the item: `agent` when the agent
  can continue, `none` when nothing waits. Keep `owner` while another of his
  questions on that item is still open.
- An item at `owner` stays in the briefing and in `toolkit work decisions`,
  and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of its next stage.
- Waiting on someone else: `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on 'external: <who>'`
  and the Overview Blockers line names what is missing.

## 6. Asking the owner

- Ask in the reply text. Never ask through a question tool (such as Codex's
  `request_user_input`): he may never see it, and the reply must hold the
  question.
- One question per message. Give your recommended answer and the main reason
  in one line, so he can confirm, correct, or redirect it.
- The one exception: more than three findings from the `work-requirements`
  spec check go in one numbered list he can answer in one message.
- Never ask him which stage an item is in, or which helpers a small item
  needs. Work those out yourself.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not an
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.

## 7. Ending every reply

End every reply to the owner with one of these:

- the one question he must answer ("Do you approve these requirements?");
- the exact words that continue the work ("Say 'keep going' and I'll start
  the build.").

Never end on "The next step is ..." with nothing for him to do.

## 8. Reporting a failed save

- The write failed: lead with "Not saved". Name what was not saved and where
  it should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified", name the line the CLI says differs, and read the item back to
  judge it.
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## 9. Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move or rename a folder, drag a
Notion card, change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, writes a history row,
and reports it. Never undo it.

- The session briefing lists these under "Changes found in the tracker", and
  every `toolkit work` command prints the ones it finds. Tell the owner each
  one in one line in the reply (not only in a progress line), before other
  work. Each line the CLI prints is written to be said as it is. Do not guess
  at a cause the CLI does not name.
- The CLI writes the history rows for a hand move. Add a note only for what it
  cannot know, such as the owner's reason.
- A hand change that skips a gate (a `build` item moved past stage 03 without
  approved requirements, or Done with no recorded result approval) is asked
  about as a question. The CLI prints the question and the command for each
  answer.

## 10. Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`: "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item waits for.

## 11. Handing over to another skill

- Claude Code: open the skill with the Skill tool, by name.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path in the skill list, then
  follow it.
- Say the handover in one line: "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`. The
  delivery offer is the exception: only `work-delegate` records it.

# Work item and design format

What a work item and its design hold, their exact section names, and how to
change them with `toolkit work` commands without losing text.

## Contents

1. Where the record and the design live
2. Header fields
3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`
4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`
5. Finding an item's file
6. Changing one section
7. Adding a table row
8. Editing a record directly
9. Titles
10. Generated files
11. Examples

## 1. Where the record and the design live

Every tracker uses the same body and the same design shape. Only the place
differs.

| Tracker | Work item | Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local | `WORK-ITEM.md` in the item's folder under `.work-items/` | `DESIGN.md` beside it |
| Notion | The item's page in the project's Work Items database | The item's "Solution Design" child page |
| GitHub Issues | The issue body | One issue comment whose first line is `## Solution design` |
| Jira | The issue description | One comment whose first line is "Solution design" |

An item has one design home. Never make a separate design folder or a second
design file.

## 2. Header fields

The header (frontmatter locally, properties in Notion) holds these fields.
Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

| Field | Values | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `WI-001` (the project's prefix and a number) | `toolkit work new`; never reused |
| `title` | The owner's words for the request | `toolkit work set <id> --title` |
| `type` | `discovery`, `solution-design`, `build`, `data-load`, `repository-maintenance`, `research`, `task`, `bug`, `enhancement`, or another lower-case word | `toolkit work set <id> --type` |
| `stage` | `01-discovery` to `14-spec-update` | `toolkit work set <id> --stage`, `approve`, `finish`, `cancel` |
| `status` | Backlog, Ready, In Progress, In Review, Done, Cancelled | Follows the stage; Done and Cancelled only through `finish` and `cancel` |
| `parent` | An item id or `none` | `toolkit work new --parent`, `toolkit work move` |
| `waiting_on` | `owner`, `agent`, `external: <who>`, `none` | `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on` |
| `priority` | `urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low` | `toolkit work set <id> --priority` |
| `delivery` | `agent-led`, `owner-led`, `not-offered` | `toolkit work set <id> --delivery` |
| `requirements_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements` |
| `design` | `proposed`, `approved`, `superseded`, `none` | `toolkit work design`, `toolkit work approve <id> --design` |
| `result_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --result`, `toolkit work finish --quote` |
| `updated` | `YYYY-MM-DD` | Every `toolkit work` write |

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stage labels, the statuses, and the types.
Blocked is not a status: an item that cannot move has `waiting_on` set and its
Overview Blockers line filled.

## 3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` takes. A `###` subsection can be named on
its own, for example `--section 'Agreed goal'`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | The phase table: Phase (`P1 — <name>`), Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | One `### P1 — <name>` heading per phase, with checkbox tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: Date, Change or decision, Effect on the work (newest first) |
| `Open Questions` | Rows: ID (`Q-01`), Question, Affects, Status, Decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status and Finalization rule, then the subsections below |
| `Starting request` | The owner's own words for the request |
| `Agreed goal` | The outcome the owner agreed the item delivers |
| `Active requirements` | One `#### R-01 — <name>` block per requirement |
| `Acceptance` | The numbered list of what makes the whole item acceptable |
| `Notes` | The subsections below |
| `Decisions and context` | Context the next session needs that is not a requirement |
| `Resume here` | Where the next session picks up |
| `Solution options and considerations` | Build ideas, linked to an `R-xx`; never requirements |

The `R-xx` block fields are Status (Refining, Finalized, Superseded), Applies
to, Required behavior, Boundaries and exceptions, Acceptance check, Decision
record, and Open questions. Each field starts its own line.

In the local and Notion trackers, the requirements approval command sets the
Requirements "Overall status" line: never write that line by hand there.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the

# The current focus

Purpose: the format of the current focus, when to change it, and the exact
read-change-save sequence, in every memory backend.

## Contents

- What the focus is for
- The format
- What goes in each section
- When to check it
- Read, change, save
- A new project's focus
- Examples
- Checklist for a focus save

## What the focus is for

The current focus is the first thing the next session reads: the session
briefing includes it. It says what is happening now and where the next
session starts. It never repeats the tracker: a work item's status, tasks,
and history stay in the work item.

| Backend | Where the focus lives |
| --- | --- |
| Built-in | `.memory/CURRENT_FOCUS.md` in the main checkout |
| Hindsight | The document `focus` in the project's bank |
| Notion | The "Current focus" page under the project's page |

The same commands read and save it in every backend. Never edit the file or
the page by hand.

## The format

The model's format: a `# Current focus` title line, a `Last updated:` line,
then exactly four `##` sections in this order, under 50 lines in total.

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: <YYYY-MM-DD>, <source>, <person or agent>

## Now

## Waiting on the owner

## Untracked to-dos

## Next session starts with
```

What the command enforces:

- It refuses a focus that lacks one of the four sections, has another
  section, or is over 50 lines (exit code 2, nothing saved).
- It adds the title line or the `Last updated:` line when either is missing,
  and sets an older date to today. It cannot know the source or who wrote
  it, so write the line yourself.

## What goes in each section

- **Last updated:** the date, the source (for example `handoff`,
  `work-finish`, `chat`), and who wrote it (a person, or `agent`). Change it
  on every save.
- **Now:** the current outcome or area, with work item ids and titles only,
  for example `- WI-012 CSV export`. Never a status or a stage: the tracker
  holds those.
- **Waiting on the owner:** a decision or action only the owner can take
  that has no work item: what it is, who needs it, and when to check again.
  Work items that wait on him are listed by `toolkit work decisions`, not
  here. A setup step (trust the hooks in Codex, sign in to Notion with
  `ntn login`) stays only while `toolkit doctor` still reports it.
- **Untracked to-dos:** things the owner asked for that have no work item.
  When one becomes a work item, replace the line with the item's id under
  Now.
- **Next session starts with:** one entry: where to resume, what to read,
  and the next action. It is replaced at each handoff, not added to.
- Write "None." in a section with nothing in it.
- Keep it under 50 lines by replacing stale lines, never by appending. Never
  drop an owner to-do that is still open only to meet the limit.

## When to check it

Check the focus before the reply ends when:

- a work item's stage changes, or its next step changes to something the
  focus does not say. Check two things:
  1. Now lists the item (id and title). Add it when it is missing; take it
     off when the item is Done or Cancelled. For Done, take it off just
     before `toolkit work finish`, which backs up the focus as it is then.
  2. Next session starts with does not name a step that is done or no longer
     next. Replace that line with the item's real next step, in one line that
     points at the item, for example "Continue WI-012 from its Resume here:
     build P1."
- the owner asks for something with no work item (add it under Untracked
  to-dos), or a decision only he can make has no work item (Waiting on the
  owner).
- `toolkit doctor` no longer reports a setup step listed under Waiting on the
  owner (drop it).
- a session hands off (replace the one entry under Next session starts
  with).

Skip the save when nothing in the focus is wrong. Leave every line you are
not changing exactly as it is.

## Read, change, save

1. Read it with its version. The output has `text` and `version`:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --json
   ```

2. Change only the lines that need it, in the whole text, and update the
   `Last updated:` line.
3. Save the whole text with the version you read.
   Claude Code: `<file>` is `-`, with the text on standard input after a
   quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`), then a line holding only `EOF`.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>
   ```

   Codex: give the text in single quotes instead (newlines are kept), or
   use a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder and delete it after the save.
   Write an apostrophe as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the
   text. Never `'\''` in Codex: the project's command rule does not match
   that form, so the command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can
   drop the backslash.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
   ```

4. Exit code 2 with "changed since it was read" means another session saved
   the focus after you read it. Read it again, make your change in the new
   text, and save with the new version. Never save without `--expect`: that
   would silently drop the other session's change.
5. No focus yet (`version` is null): save with `--expect absent`, in the full
   format above.
6. Read it back:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus
   ```

## A new project's focus

A new project's focus still holds the model's setup text: a fill-in guide
comment under the title (`<!-- Fill-in guide: ... -->`) and an
`<angle-bracket>` prompt in every section. At the first save:

- remove the fill-in guide comment;
- replace each prompt with real content, or with "None." when there is none;
- never leave an angle-bracket prompt in a saved focus.

## Examples

A full focus:

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: 2026-09-26, handoff, agent

## Now

- WI-012 CSV export
- WI-015 Large exports (sub-item of WI-012)

## Waiting on the owner

- Pick a hosting provider before the first deploy (no work item yet); check again 2026-10-01.

## Untracked to-dos

- Email the client about the October demo.

## Next session starts with

- 2026-09-26 17:40 UTC | CSV export: continue WI-012 from its Resume here. Goal: exports finish under 10 seconds.
```

The handoff entry with a work item is a pointer only:
`<UTC date and time> | <topic>: continue <WI-id> from its Resume here. Goal: <one line>.`

With no work item, the entry is a short note: the goal or topic, where work
stopped, the first next action, limits on what may be done without the
owner, and open questions. Do not create a work item only to hold it.

## Checklist for a focus save

- [ ] Read with `--json`; you have the version.
- [ ] The `# Current focus` title and the `Last updated:` line (date,
      source, who) are there.
- [ ] Four sections, in order; "None." in each empty one.
- [ ] Work item ids and titles only; no status or stage.
- [ ] No angle-bracket prompt and no fill-in guide comment left.
- [ ] Under 50 lines; no open owner to-do dropped.
- [ ] Saved with `--expect`; read back.

Purpose: how to run a `toolkit` command in Claude Code and in Codex, how to
pass text in one, and what each exit code means. Every skill that runs a
`toolkit` command follows this file.

- Running toolkit commands
- Text in a command
- Exit codes
- Reporting a save
- Reading output and updating what you read
- Right and wrong examples

## Running toolkit commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- Why, in Codex: the project's command rule (`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules`)
  runs a `toolkit` command outside the sandbox only when it is the whole
  command. A `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion, the
  local Hindsight server, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and
  `.memory/` from a worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong
  cause.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc; "Text in a command", below).
- Five commands ask the owner first, in both hosts, because they are hard or
  impossible to undo: `toolkit machine-setup`, `toolkit memory delete`,
  `toolkit memory import`, `toolkit import`, and
  `toolkit hindsight service install` or `start`. Get his yes in the reply
  before you run one. The host then asks him to confirm the command (Claude
  Code: a permission prompt; Codex: an approval). That prompt is expected, not
  an error.
- When the host refuses one of the five without asking him (Codex with
  approvals off: "approval required by policy, but AskForApproval is set to
  Never"), say that the cause is that approval setting, show him the exact
  command to run himself in a terminal, and wait. Do nothing in its place
  that he did not ask for: a refused delete is not a retire.
- In Codex, run each of those five alone, with `sandbox_permissions` set to
  `require_escalated` and a one-line reason. The approval alone keeps the
  command inside the sandbox, where it fails: `toolkit memory delete` cannot
  reach Hindsight or Notion, `toolkit machine-setup` cannot write `~/.codex`
  or `~/.local/bin`, `toolkit hindsight service install` cannot write
  `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and `toolkit import` from a worktree cannot write
  the main checkout.
- Write `--json` and `--host` after the command words
  (`toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved --json`). The toolkit refuses
  those five commands when a flag comes first, because the ask-first rules
  would not match them.
- Never change a work item or a memory record with a script or a shell write
  (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`, `tee`, `cp`). Use the `toolkit` command
  that owns it. The hooks refuse the shell write, so it only wastes a step.
- `toolkit help <command>` prints every option of one command.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still reports success. So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Never use double quotes for text.
- **An apostrophe inside single quotes:**
  - Claude Code: write it as `'\''`, for example
    `--note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`.
  - Codex: write it as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the text.
    Never `'\''` in Codex: the command rule does not match that form, so the
    command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can drop the
    backslash, which leaves a quote that is never closed.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere.
  Claude Code refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary file there
  could never be deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line
  holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --set-file - <<'EOF'
  <the whole section text>
  EOF
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text:
  1. Make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d`. Its name is
     unique, so two sessions or two projects never share a file.
  2. Write the file in it with the file edit tool (`apply_patch`).
  3. Run the `toolkit` command alone, with the file's full path.
  4. Delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds
     (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything.

  Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
  ```

- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`. Every
  project starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this
  item.
- Never leave a draft file inside `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. A second
  `DESIGN.md`-shaped file there confuses the design lookup, and a stray note
  in `.memory/` is read as a memory.

`toolkit help work` prints them as: "0 ok, 1 error, 2 validation failure or a
refused gate, 3 not supported for this tracker, 4 not a toolkit project."
`toolkit help memory` uses the same numbers: "1 error or not found, 2 refused
(a rule or a stale --expect), 3 not supported by this backend".

| `0` | Done. | Read back what you wrote before you report it as saved ("Reporting a save", below). A "Note:" line in the output still needs action: report it to the owner, or do what it says. |

# Writing a requirement

How to write an `R-xx` block and the Acceptance list so someone who was not
in the conversation can build and check the result.

## What a requirement says

- Plain words, no jargon. State the goal, what people must be able to do,
  what must happen, and the rules that govern it.
- Each requirement says what must be true and why, never how to build it. No
  file paths, versions, tool choices, or build steps in a requirement.
- Make behavior explicit: who is affected, when the rule applies, the
  expected result, and the exceptions.
- Every requirement has an acceptance check someone can observe.
- Use only settled details. Leave missing decisions open as questions.

## The `R-xx` block

From the work item template. The name follows an em dash. Each field starts
its own line, and every line but the last ends with two spaces.

```markdown
#### R-01 — Rejected requests show their reason

**Status:** Refining  
**Applies to:** The person who submitted a request, after it is rejected.  
**Required behavior:** The requester can see the rejection reason on the request.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** Requests withdrawn by the requester have no reason.  
**Acceptance check:** Reject a request with a reason; the requester sees that reason on the request.  
**Decision record:** Owner, 2026-09-26, interview.  
**Open questions:** None.
```

- Status words: Refining, Finalized, Superseded.
- A new or changed requirement is Refining until the owner approves it.
- After his approval: Status Finalized, and the Decision record adds who
  approved it and when ("Approved by Mike on 2026-09-28."). Do this for every
  approved block in one edit of `Active requirements`.
- A superseded requirement keeps its block, with Status Superseded and the id
  of the `R-xx` that replaced it in its Decision record.
- A changed approved requirement keeps its old wording in its Decision record
  ("Was: ... Changed by the owner on 2026-09-28.").
- Numbers are never reused. A new requirement takes the next free `R-` number.

Save the whole subsection:

```text
toolkit work show <id> --section 'Active requirements'
toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Active requirements' --set-file <file>
```

## The Acceptance list

The Acceptance subsection says when the whole item can be accepted: the
result, how it is checked, and any owner review.

```markdown
This work item can be accepted when:

1. Managers can download the monthly report as a CSV file.
2. The file opens in Excel with every column the report shows (R-01, R-02).
3. The owner has tried one export himself.
```

## Build ideas are not requirements

Ideas about how to build something go under Notes > Solution options and
considerations, linked to the `R-xx` they relate to. They are neither
requirements nor an approved design.

```markdown
- **For R-01:** A page message or an email are possible ways to show the reason.
```

## Lines never written by hand

In the local and Notion trackers, the requirements approval command sets the
Requirements "Overall status" line. Never write Finalized there yourself.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Finalized there (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`).

## Checks before asking for approval

- [ ] Every `R-xx` has all seven fields filled, with no template prompt left.
- [ ] Every acceptance check can be observed by someone else.

# Approvals and gates

The exact steps to ask for and record each owner approval, and what counts as
one. Run each checklist in order; one wrong or missing command leaves the
item in the wrong state.

## Contents

1. What counts as approval
2. Requirements approval
3. Design approval
4. Result approval
5. Done
6. Cancel
7. Delivery offer
8. Project-wide decision
9. Memory proposal
10. Sub-items and approvals
11. Standing merge instruction
12. When an approve command refuses

## 1. What counts as approval

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the gates and these rules. In short:

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in a history note.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), silence, or a
  saved draft is not approval.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment,
  spending, or publishing.
- An approval survives later stages. A stage alone does not prove approval:
  check the approval field (`toolkit work show <id>`).
- A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" answers only a yes-or-no question asked
  earlier in this conversation. When none was asked, or the waiting question
  is not a yes-or-no question, show the decision with its choices and your
  recommendation, and record nothing.
- After a yes, save his words first, in a history note that starts with
  `Owner said:`. Then run the gate's commands. A command that refuses then
  never loses his answer, and no later session asks him again.
- `--by <owner>` is his name exactly as `toolkit config get project.owner`
  prints it (for example "Mike Rihm", not "Mike"), so every approval names
  him the same way.
- When an approve command notes that the item's Overview still asks for
  that approval (Next action), write the step after the approval with the
  `toolkit work edit` command the note prints.

| The owner says | After this question | It is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Yes, approved." | "Do you approve these requirements?" | The requirements approval |
| "Go with B." | The design options with a recommendation | The choice and approval of Option B |
| "Looks good." | "Do you approve this result?" | The result approval |
| "Looks good." | "Shall I split WI-12 into these three sub-items?" | A yes to the split only, not a result approval |
| "ok" | Nothing was asked in this chat | Not an answer; ask what he wants |
| "Probably A, but let me think." | The design options | Not an answer; the design stays proposed |
| "Ship it." | He has seen the result, gaps, and evidence | The result approval (record it with his words) |

## 2. Requirements approval

Asked by `work-requirements`. `work-decide` records a later answer.

Before asking:

- [ ] The Agreed goal holds real text. The CLI refuses the approval while it
      still holds the template text.
- [ ] The spec check ran (`requirements-analyst`), and its findings were fixed
      or turned into questions.
- [ ] No Open Questions row linked to a requirement is still open. If one is,
      say which and ask it first.

Ask: show the Agreed goal, each requirement in one line, the Acceptance list,
and any open question. Then ask exactly "Do you approve these requirements?"
as the last line, and set the item waiting on the owner.

```text
toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner
```

After his yes, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first, so no later session asks him again.
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approved.'`
- [ ] Set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and add who approved it and
      when to its Decision record, in one edit of `Active requirements`.
      `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Active requirements' --set-file <file>`
- [ ] Record the approval. It adds its own history row, marks the Open
      Questions rows that asked for it Answered, sets `waiting_on` to `none`,
      and moves an earlier item to stage 03.
      `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
- [ ] Hand the item back to the agent, unless another question for him is
      still open on it.
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- [ ] Check the record.
      `toolkit work validate <id>`
- [ ] Next: a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless the
      owner agreed to skip the design. Say a skip in the final reply, not in a
      progress line.

Not yet, or a change: the item stays waiting on him. Record the change and
ask again.

A yes that arrives later (`work-decide` records it):

- The Agreed goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown
  with the approval question, then record the approval.
  `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Agreed goal' --text '<goal he was shown>'`
- A requirement still has a linked open question: say which one, open
  `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval once it is answered,
  without asking him again.

## 3. Design approval

Asked by `solution-design`. `work-decide` records a later answer.

Before asking:

- [ ] The design is saved as proposed, and the item waits on the owner. Add no
      Open Questions row for the design approval itself: a proposed design is
      already listed as his decision.
      `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file> --status proposed`
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`

Ask: the options in one sentence each, your recommendation and its reason,
what he will see when it is done, the main risks, and the build order. Then
ask him to choose or approve.

After his yes, or his choice of one option, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first, so no later session asks him again.
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Design approved; work-on plans the build.'`
- [ ] Fill "Recommendation and owner decision": Owner decision (who, when,
      where he said it) and Reason for decision (his reason only; never invent
      one).
- [ ] Fill every "Selected design" subsection and the "Build and verification
      plan" (Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks with one row per
      requirement). `work-check` reads those checks.
- [ ] Remove every leftover template prompt. Leave the Design status line as
      it is.
- [ ] Save the design text.
      `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file>`
- [ ] Record the approval. It adds its own history row. It refuses (exit
      code 2, `design_not_filled`) while "Selected design" still says
      "Pending owner decision" or holds the template prompt: save the filled
      design first, then run it again, without asking him again.
      `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
- [ ] Hand the item back to the agent, unless another question is still open.
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- [ ] Check the record.
      `toolkit work validate <id>`

He wants changes: record them in the design's Notes > Design changes during
the interview, run a fix round for the named changes only, save it as
proposed again, and ask again.

## 4. Result approval

Asked by `work-check` at stage 11.

Before asking:

- [ ] The tests and every acceptance check ran, and an independent checker
      reported, or you say plainly that no independent check ran.
- [ ] The check is recorded in a history note (what was checked, the
      evidence, the gaps).
- [ ] The item is at stage 11 and waits on the owner. Add no Open Questions
      row: stage 11 already lists the result as his decision.
      `toolkit work set <id> --stage 11-user-approval --waiting-on owner`

Ask: what it does now in his terms, how he can see it himself, the evidence,
and the gaps. Then ask exactly "Do you approve this result?" Never hide a gap
to get a yes.

After his yes, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first.
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
- [ ] Record the approval.
      `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
- [ ] Hand the item back to the agent.
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- [ ] Open `work-finish`.

A "no": record his words, turn each problem he names into a task or a
requirement change, and continue checking.

## 5. Done

Asked by `work-finish`. Only `toolkit work finish` sets Done.

Before the finish command:

- [ ] The result approval is recorded, or you have the owner's own words
      approving this result to pass with `--quote`.
- [ ] Every change the item made is committed and reached the default branch,
      or the owner said to leave it on the branch.
- [ ] Requirements and system guide updates are saved through `publish-docs`.
- [ ] Every open sub-item is finished, cancelled, or moved, or the owner said
      the parent is done anyway.
- [ ] Every Roadmap phase the item completed says Done.
- [ ] Overview: Related items current, Current position "Done on <date>:
      <evidence>", Blockers "None.".
- [ ] Leftover worktrees and branches for the item are listed and offered for
      removal.

Then run one of these:

```text
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>' --quote '<his exact words>'
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>' --allow-open-sub-items
```

The second is only for a result approval not yet recorded. The third is only
for a parent the owner said is done while sub-items are still open; quote his
words in a history note. The command sets Next action and Resume here, and
prints what still needs a note.

The finish command also backs up `.work-items/` and `.memory/` (and Hindsight
memory) to the owner's backup folder and prints one line about it. Read that
line:

- "Backed up ... to <folder>": done. Say it in one line in the reply.
- "No backup folder is set ...": ask the owner for a folder outside the
  project, as a question in the reply. After his answer:
  `toolkit config set backup.dir <folder>` (or `none` when he wants no backup).
- A line with "failed" or "Tell the owner": tell him that line as it is. The
  item is still Done; only the backup is missing.

## 6. Cancel

Asked by `work-finish`. Only `toolkit work cancel` sets Cancelled.

- [ ] The reason is the owner's own words, not a summary.
- [ ] Each open sub-item: ask whether to cancel it, move it to the top level,
      or move it under another item. Never cancel them without asking.
- [ ] `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`

Cancelling keeps the record. Nothing is deleted.

## 7. Delivery offer

Only `work-delegate` makes the offer and records the answer. Every other skill
opens `work-delegate` for it. The recorded value:

```text
toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led
toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led
```

A delivery answer never approves requirements, a design, or a result, and
never widens merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.

## 8. Project-wide decision

Recorded by `work-decide` as a row in `DECISIONS.md` at the project root,
then committed through `publish-docs`.

```text
toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>
toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>
```

`DECISIONS.md` is append-only. A changed decision is a new row that names the
one it replaces. Any skill that meets a project-wide decision opens
`work-decide`, which runs the full order of work with `publish-docs`.

## 9. Memory proposal

A memory the owner did not answer ("Save to memory?") is saved as a proposal:
status `needs-review`. The agent does not rely on it until he approves it.

```text
toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>
toolkit memory reject <key>
```

A rejection deletes the proposal. Never propose the same fact again in other
words.

## 10. Sub-items and approvals

- A child made with `--covers R-02,R-03` links those parent requirements and
  inherits the parent's requirements approval. The owner is never asked to
  approve the same requirement twice.
- A parent design the owner approved covers its `--covers` children: they
  start at planning (stage 06) with no design of their own.
- A child that needs new behavior gets its own `R-xx` and its own approval.
- Each sub-item needs its own result approval. The owner's approval of the
  parent does not cover it.
- Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.

## 11. Standing merge instruction

A merge normally needs the owner's yes to that merge. A standing merge
instruction replaces that yes only when all of these hold:

- [ ] `DECISIONS.md` records it as the owner's decision (the project's
      `AGENTS.md` may point at it);
- [ ] an `acceptance-checker` that did not build the change reported no
      blocking issue on that exact head commit;
- [ ] every check passes on that head;
- [ ] the work item does not say its merge needs the owner's approval (an
      item that says so overrides the instruction).

Without an independent check the instruction does not apply: ask the owner.
A new commit after the check means a new check on the new head.

## 12. When an approve command refuses

- Show the owner the command's error in plain words. Never work around it by
  editing the record, the design text, or a header field.
- The error names what is missing (for example the Agreed goal still holds
  the template text). Fix that, then run the same command again.
- Exit code 2 means a refused gate: the record is unchanged.

description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in the project''s memory, or sends it to the record where it belongs. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "forget that", or "remind me" with no time given, corrects the agent, or a hook says a save is due.'

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Saves, corrects, or retires one memory record with `toolkit memory` commands, or sends the fact to its proper home. It never edits memory files by hand.

## Steps

Track these steps in the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

1. Decide the home with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory, which wins; otherwise `references/memory-criteria.md`). Not memory: send it to its home ("Where other things go" below) and stop.
2. Search for a record that already holds it, and read each hit with its version. The save's duplicate check compares wording, so only this search finds a record the new fact contradicts (for example "Mondays" against "Tuesdays").
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Read the approval mode and apply "Approval policy" below. When it says ask, ask and wait.
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
4. Write the description and body in the record format (`references/record-format.md`), then save with the form for the case ("Save forms" below).
5. Exit code 2 saved nothing. Read the "Error:" line. Records listed: the duplicate check. "Changed since it was read": read it again and redo the change. Any other rule: fix the text as the message says. `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 2, has each case.
6. "Forget that": retire the record, with his words as the reason. Delete only when his own words say delete ("Approval policy").
   `toolkit memory retire <key> --reason '<his words>'`
7. An owner to-do with no work item, or a change to what is happening now: update the current focus (`references/current-focus.md`). A project term: update the glossary (`references/glossary.md`).
8. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
9. Read the record back, check, and reply in one line ("Replies" below). End with the question still waiting for the owner, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Approval policy

This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy.

- The owner's own words are the approval: "remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", or a correction. Save now, with `--approved-by <owner>`. That includes a fact about a named person he asks you to remember ("remember that Priya's last day is October 15").
- `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first, in exactly this form: "Save to memory: <one-line summary>?". Save after his yes (`references/proposals.md` when a proposal was saved for the question).
- A preference or fact he mentions in passing, without a keep phrase or an instruction ("screenshots were more useful than the text"), is inferred: ask "Save to memory: ...?" first. Only his keep words, or his yes to that question, are an approval.
- Recommend a yes only with evidence from this project (what he said, what happened, and when). With none, ask without a recommendation.
- `trusted` mode: a routine fact the agent is sure of is saved without asking and reported in one line, with no approver. The record says "Trusted grant".
- In either mode, always ask first for anything about a named person or personal details that he did not ask you to remember, for more than five records at once, and for a change to this policy.
- A delete needs his own words about that record ("delete it", "remove it for good"), or his yes to a numbered list that shows the delete. Do not ask again: the host asks him to confirm `toolkit memory delete`, and that prompt is the confirmation. "Forget that" is a retire, never a delete.
- A yes covers only the change and the meaning shown. Silence is never a yes.
- `--approved-by` is only for a change his words or his yes covered. Give his name exactly as the project settings hold it (`project.owner`, for example "Mike Rihm", not "Mike").
- An unanswered "Save to memory?" stays a proposal until he answers (`references/proposals.md`). Never drop it, and never save it with an approver.
- Only the owner switches the mode, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date, then run one of:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`

## Save forms

`<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the body on standard input after a quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`). In Codex give `--body '<text>'` in place of `--body-file <file>`. `references/record-format.md` shows both.

- A new record, from the owner's words or his yes:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
- A new routine fact in `trusted` mode:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>'`
- A question he has not answered yet:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --proposal`
- An update of a record read in step 2, which his words or his yes covered:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
- A routine update in `trusted` mode (the stored authorization is kept):
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version>`
- A new record that replaces an old one: add `--supersedes <old-key>` to a new-record form.
- A better name, or a type that matches the content:
  `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script. In Codex a joined command runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight, Notion, and the main checkout's `.memory/`.
- Put one-line values (`--description`, `--source`, `--reason`) in single quotes. An apostrophe inside them: Claude Code writes `'\''`; Codex writes ’ (U+2019) or rewords, and never uses `'\''`, which runs the command inside the sandbox. Double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`, drop that text, and the save still says "Saved".
- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/memory.md`, and never write a file and run the command in one shell command.
- Body labels are bold paragraphs (`**Remember:**`), never `## Remember` headings.
- **Why** is the owner's reason in his words, or exactly "Not stated by the owner." Never a reason you inferred.
- In `onboarding` mode, a save with neither `--approved-by` nor `--proposal` is stored as "No approval recorded", and the save prints a "Note:" line about it. That is a mistake: fix it at once. Ask him, then save again with `--expect` and `--approved-by` after his yes, or with `--proposal` while he has not answered.
- A save of an existing key without `--expect` saves nothing. Take the version from the `--json` read; the first 12 characters are enough. Keep that read: its old text is the undo for an update.
- Add `--allow-similar` only after reading every record the duplicate check listed.
- A proposal the Stop hook saved holds only the one-line summary. His plain yes is `toolkit memory approve`, which takes out its "Do not rely on this" words; when he adds a reason or a detail, save the full body instead (`references/proposals.md`).
- Never store email addresses, secrets, or work-item status. The CLI catches common secret shapes, not all. For a secret, save where it is kept, never the secret.
- Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- Say "proposal" only for a record saved with `--proposal` (by you or the Stop hook). When nothing was saved, say that nothing was saved, and ask.
- An inferred fact whose home is a project document (for example `PROJECT.md`) is asked the same way, as one yes-or-no line: "Add to PROJECT.md: <one line>?". When he does not answer, add it to the current focus under "Waiting on the owner", so it is asked again (`references/current-focus.md`).
- The host refused `toolkit memory delete` without asking him (Codex with approvals off): the cause is that approval setting. Show him the exact command to run in a terminal and wait. Do not retire the record in its place unless he asks for that.
- Built-in memory: the CLI rebuilds `MEMORY.md` and repairs links in other notes after a rename, supersede, retire, or delete, and names each note it changed. Read that report (`references/memory-builtin.md`).

A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy the record's body.

## Replies

Use these lines word for word, with the record's title. Every memory reply ends with the next step: the question still waiting for the owner (for example "Save to memory: <one line>?"), or the exact words that continue. Never end on what was not done ("I haven't saved anything.").

- A new record: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo."
- An update: "Updated in memory: <title>. Say 'undo that' to put back the old wording." His "undo that" is a save of the old text from the `--json` read (`references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 3). Right after a supersede, the undo is a restore of the old record and a retire of the new one (same file, section 4).
- A proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."
- A rejected proposal: "Not saved: <title>. I will not suggest it again.", then the next step.
- A retire: "Retired from memory: <title>. Say 'bring it back' to restore it." His "bring it back" is the whole restore in `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 7, not `toolkit memory restore` alone.
- A delete: "Deleted from memory, as you said: '<his words>'. This cannot be undone." For a secret or an email address, add that older backups still hold it (`references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 8).
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved: <reason>." Keep the text and try again later in the session. With Hindsight or Notion, the command prints the fix (`references/memory-hindsight.md`, `references/memory-notion.md`).

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds one line when the owner's message holds one of six keep phrases: "remember that" (or "remember this"), "from now on", "don't ever", "note that", "going forward", or "keep in mind". It is a reminder: route the fact with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase got no save, work-item change, or decision in the turn. Save it, or say in one line where it went instead.
- Ask in exactly the form "Save to memory: <one line>?" (bold is fine). Other wording, such as "Save it to memory?", makes the Stop hook stop the turn once and ask for that form.
- When a reply asks "Save to memory: <summary>?" and no proposal was saved in that turn, the Stop hook tries to save one, and the next turn's context says what happened:
  - It saved a proposal and names its key: his yes approves that key, his no rejects it (`references/proposals.md`, "Recording the owner's answer").
  - Memory already holds a proposal like it, and names it: his answer approves or rejects that proposal.
  - Memory already holds a record about the same subject, and names it: read it as in step 2. The same fact: keep it, or update it with `--expect`. A different fact and his yes: save it with `--allow-similar` and `--approved-by`. Never overwrite a record with a different fact.
  - The text looks like a secret, so nothing was saved: never save it; after his yes, save only where the secret is kept.
  - The save failed: save the proposal yourself in this turn, with `--proposal`.
